title: What all share: the truths
hook: every school teaches the four truths and the eightfold path

segments.voice: Yesterday, movements: the raft that is for crossing, not for carrying, and the many schools we've met. Your line was many ways. Which one did you name? Day one thousand three hundred sixty.

In Pali, in a monastery in Sri Lanka. In classical Chinese, in a temple in Taipei. In Tibetan, in a dharma hall in the Himalayas. In English, in a Zen center on a rainy evening. Different robes, different bells, different languages. And yet, listen closely to what the teachers explain to new students, and the same short list keeps surfacing, the one the Buddha is said to have given in his very first teaching. We spent weeks on the differences between the schools. Now a new block begins: the schools side by side, ranked by no one. We start with what they hold in common. Today: what all share.
screen: `PALI, CHINESE, TIBETAN, ENGLISH.` → `THE SAME SHORT LIST.` → `SIDE BY SIDE.`

segments.voice: First, where it starts. The discourse called Setting in Motion the Wheel of the Dhamma tells how the Buddha, after his awakening, went to the Deer Park near Benares and spoke to his old companions, a talk tradition counts as his first. Rhys Davids' translation has him name "the noble truth concerning suffering." Then three more follow. Second, the four truths. There is suffering, dukkha: the ache, the unsatisfactoriness that runs through life. It has an arising: craving, the thirst that grasps. It has an ending: when the craving is let go, the suffering stops. And there is a way to that ending. Third, the way itself: the noble eightfold path. Right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, right concentration. Not eight steps to climb in order, teachers say, but eight strands of one rope. Fourth, how the schools hold them. Across the schools this course has visited, the four truths and the eightfold path turn up again and again. Theravada teaching keeps them close to the center, in the words of the Pali discourses. Mahayana teachers keep them too, and some read them through emptiness: the Heart Sutra, a short text chanted in Mahayana temples, goes so far as to say there is no suffering, no arising, no ending and no path. Its teachers explain this not as throwing the truths away, but as holding even them without grasping. Some Tibetan teachers place the four truths at the beginning of the path, as the ground everything else stands on. Same truths, held in different hands. That's the shape of this whole block: what they share, and where they differ, without a winner.
screen: `THE DEER PARK, THE FIRST TEACHING.` · `SUFFERING, ARISING, ENDING, WAY.` · `EIGHT STRANDS OF ONE ROPE.` · `SAME TRUTHS, DIFFERENT HANDS.` · then, large: `SHARED BY ALL.`

segments.voice: Four out-breaths, four short lines, if you'd like to try it. Let the breath settle first. Then say the four truths once more, slowly, one on each out-breath. There is suffering. Breathe. Suffering has an arising. Breathe. Suffering has an ending. Breathe. There is a way. Then sit quietly, and let the eight strands of the path come to mind, one by one, without trying to remember them perfectly. Notice which one feels closest today: speech, perhaps, or effort, or mindfulness. Rest there. The bell holds the time.
What all share. The four noble truths and the eightfold path, taught across the Buddhist schools in their own languages and their own ways. Today's word.
Your line: shared by all. Today, when something aches, try naming it the old way: suffering, its arising, its ending, the way. Day one thousand three hundred sixty.

howItsDone: Teachers in the Buddhist schools teach the four noble truths and the eightfold path to beginners, and Buddhists chant or recite them, in Pali, Chinese, Tibetan, Japanese, English and other languages.

original.note: Pali ariyasacca: noble truth. The four noble truths are cattari ariyasaccani.

trapdoor: what you thought: each Buddhist school teaches something completely different.
what it means: the schools share the four truths and the eightfold path, though they hold them in different ways.
what a scholar hears: the first discourse in the Deer Park, kept at the center by Theravada, read through emptiness in the Heart Sutra, laid as the ground in Tibetan teaching.

notes: Editor: "first teaching" now attributed to tradition (the cited sutta names Benares and the Deer Park, not "first"); "Tibetan teachers often" softened to "some Tibetan teachers"; Theravada line no longer generalizes about all teachers; varied the practice opener.
Index hook says 'every school teaches'; script softens to 'across the schools this course has visited, they turn up again and again' under the claims rule. Confirm.
